extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of history of mathematics; readers interested in Greek mathematics and the origins of Euclidean methods
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and interpreting standards, methods and evaluative points from a scholarly historical account of Greek mathematicians (e.g. Plato's school, Eudoxus, Archimedes) and their mathematical practices. Emphasis on methodological, conceptual and historiographical criteria that the author highlights as important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisite knowledge for entry to the Academy
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who would enter Plato's school were required to have a knowledge of music, geometry and astronomy; otherwise they were dismissed ('Go thy way, for thou hast not the means of getting a grip of philosophy').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an admission/eligibility standard — indicates that a certain technical background was judged necessary to engage with the school's mathematical-philosophical work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of propositions: theorem vs problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Different authors classified the same items differently: e.g. Proclus reports that Speusippus regarded both theorems and problems alike as 'more properly theorems', while Menaechmus would call both alike 'problems'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows that labeling (theorem vs problem) affects mathematical presentation and possibly method; evaluators should note the classificatory conventions used by an author when assessing their work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine conditions for possibility (Siopia-fios / diorismi)
rubrics_metrics.description: The recognition of the necessity of finding, as a preliminary to the solution of a problem, the conditions for the possibility of a solution (di-orismi or Siopia-fios).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a methodological standard: before attempting construction/proof, identify solvability conditions and constraints. Leon's invention of diorismi exemplifies this advance in mathematical technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generality of theorems / making partial theorems more general
rubrics_metrics.description: A merit in mathematicians like Eudoxus and Theudius was to increase the number of 'general theorems' and to make many partial (or limited) theorems more general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value is placed on extending results from special cases to broader classes of magnitudes or figures; collectors/compilers of elements were judged by number of propositions proved and their utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addition and classification of means/proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond the arithmetic, geometric and harmonic means, further 'proportions' (means) were added and attributed to later investigators; these additions were counted as substantive advances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative attention should be given to the extension of proportion theory (new kinds of means) and to claims of attribution — check sources and competing attributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory of proportion applicable to incommensurables
rubrics_metrics.description: The new theory (Euclid Book V) offers a general theory of proportion equally applicable to geometry, arithmetic, music and all mathematical science; its essence is applicability to incommensurable as well as commensurable quantities (Eucl. V, Def. 4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is treated as a decisive methodological advance: definitions and proofs must work for incommensurables; correspondence with later formulations (Dedekind/Weierstrass) is noted as evidence of rigor and generality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of analysis followed by synthesis (analytic method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying the method of analysis to problems about 'the section' and providing alternative proofs in the form 'analysis followed by synthesis' (as reported for propositions in Euclid XIII).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological standard: produce an analytic derivation to identify necessary steps/conditions, then a synthetic demonstration; watch for interpolations in manuscripts that may conflate later pedagogical additions with original practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of exhaustion as rigorous limiting proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The method of exhaustion (used to prove area/volume relations) — associated with Eudoxus and later Archimedes — uses a lemma/axiom (Archimedes's lemma / Eucl. V, Def. 4) enabling reductio ad absurdum style proofs rather than informal limiting arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish rigorous exhaustion proofs from heuristic 'quadrature' arguments. Preference is given to demonstrations that employ explicit lemmas and reductio-style rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of explicit lemmas/axioms to justify limiting arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Employment of explicit lemmas (e.g. Archimedes's lemma equivalently Eucl. V Def. 4; Euclid X.1 lemma about repeatedly subtracting halves) is required to underpin proofs about circles, pyramids, cones and spheres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize these lemmas as the technical foundations enabling rigorous proofs of measure relations; their presence or absence distinguishes rigorous from informal arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical demonstration preferred over non-rigorous argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Hippocrates's earlier proofs may have 'contained the germ' of methods but lacked the full rigor that Eudoxus/Archimedes required; Eudoxus is credited with supplying 'scientific proof' where earlier geometers used non-rigorous methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical evaluation privileges rigorous demonstration; when assessing claims of priority or method, check whether proofs meet the criteria of exhaustion/axiomatic justification rather than only intuitive limiting procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminological and textual clarity (e.g., meaning of 'section')
rubrics_metrics.description: Debates about the meaning of terms such as 'section' (whether it means division of a straight line in extreme and mean ratio or sections of solids by planes) affect interpretation of who discovered what and how.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholarly judgments should attend closely to original wording, singular/plural usage, manuscript evidence and alternative readings; ambiguous terminology can lead to divergent reconstructions of mathematical development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical-critical standards for attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Caution about accepting attributions or apparently original material when definitions/proofs may be interpolations by scholiasts (e.g., alternative proofs and definitions interpolated into Euclid XIII).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require manuscript-based evidence and philological scrutiny before attributing discoveries; be skeptical of later insertions presented as original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory adequacy of mathematical hypotheses (astronomical models)
rubrics_metrics.description: Astronomical hypotheses (Eudoxus's concentric homocentric spheres) are judged by their ability, purely on geometric hypotheses, to account for observed phenomena (daily rotation, stations, retrogradations, nodal motions, inclinations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate models by whether their geometric/mechanical assumptions produce the entire set of observed motions; mathematical reproducibility of phenomena is a key criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parsimony and constructive simplicity in models
rubrics_metrics.description: Eudoxus adopted circular motion and concentric spheres; success included producing planetary phenomena with a minimal set of motions/spheres (three for sun/moon, four for planets in general).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor models that explain phenomena with simple, uniform assumptions (e.g., uniform circular motions) and minimal additional constructs, provided they retain explanatory power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric constructibility and use of spatial intersections/curves
rubrics_metrics.description: Solutions of algebraic/metric problems by constructing and intersecting curves and surfaces (e.g., conic sections for two mean proportionals, quadratrix for squaring the circle, intersections of torus/cylinder/cone) are accepted methods of solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value geometric creativity: using three-dimensional constructions and curve intersections to produce solutions. When evaluating a proposed solution, consider whether the required constructions are within the acceptable geometric toolkit of the period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting and combinatorial reasoning as legitimate mathematical method
rubrics_metrics.description: The anecdote that Xenocrates tried to compute the number of syllables formable from alphabet letters (1,002,000,000,000) exemplifies early attempts to solve permutation/combination problems by counting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize combinatorial enumeration as a valid strand of mathematical inquiry in antiquity; treat such attempts as early manifestations of systematic counting methods.
